title: Heart of Darkness
description: Marlow's night journey up an African river to find the ivory agent Kurtz: the central European text about empire, and one of the great English novellas.
plot_or_argument: Marlow, a riverboat captain, sits on the deck of the Nellie on the Thames and tells the story of a journey up the Congo to fetch Kurtz, the company's most successful agent, who has installed himself as a god among the local people and has gone mad. Marlow finds him dying and hears his last words — 'The horror! The horror!' — and returns to Europe carrying his memory.
narrative_structure: Three-part serial narrative framed by Marlow's narration aboard the Nellie; a journey structure with a descent into the interior.
principal_characters: Charles Marlow; Mr Kurtz; the Intended; the Manager; the Harlequin; the Accountant
literary_form: Novella (three-part serial, Blackwood's Magazine 1899; book form in Youth, 1902)
historical_context: The Congo Free State of Leopold II, where Conrad himself served as a river captain in 1890 and saw the rubber and ivory system at first hand; the book appeared in the year of the Boer War, at the height of the imperial confidence it dismantles.
literary_significance: Heart of Darkness is the indispensable European text about empire and one of the founding works of modern fiction: it invented the colonial journey narrative that the century would find endless uses for, gave the language 'the horror', and its technique — the framed narrator, the delayed disclosure, the symbolic river — made Marlow the model for the modern unreliable narrator. Chinua Achebe's attack on it in 1977 made it the centre of the debate about the colonial canon, which is itself part of its record.

title: Lord Jim
description: The story of a young first mate who abandons a sinking ship and spends the rest of his life trying to recover his honour.
plot_or_argument: Jim, the chief mate of the Patna, jumps from the ship with the officers when it seems certain to sink with 800 pilgrims aboard; the ship does not sink, and Jim is publicly disgraced at the inquiry. He moves from port to port, and finally to Patusan, a remote Malayan settlement, where he becomes 'Tuan Jim' and the trusted ruler of the people — until the pirate Gentleman Brown's raid and the death of Dain Waris destroy him, and he goes to his death willingly.
narrative_structure: Non-linear retrospective narration: Marlow's oral account framed by a third-person narrator, with letters and reports inserted.
principal_characters: Jim; Charles Marlow; Captain Brierly; Doramin; Dain Waris; Jewel; Gentleman Brown
historical_context: The age of sail's last years and the Malay Archipelago of the 1880s; the code of the sea, the merchant marine inquiry and the imperial adventurer. Conrad's own experience as a master mariner and his reading of the East gave the novel its exact detail.
literary_significance: Lord Jim is Conrad's greatest novel and one of the finest studies of moral failure in English: it made 'one of us' a permanent phrase, invented the technique of the multiple retrospective narration (Marlow collecting Jim's story from others), and gave the twentieth-century novel its central subject — the man who fails his own code and cannot be forgiven. It is the bridge between the Victorian sea story and the modern psychological novel.

title: Nostromo: A Tale of the Seaboard
description: The great political novel of South America: a silver mine, a revolution and the corruption of every ideal in the imaginary republic of Costaguana.
plot_or_argument: In the fictional South American republic of Costaguana, Charles Gould inherits the San Tomé silver mine and devotes his life to making it productive. When a revolution threatens, the silver is sent to sea with Nostromo, the Italian foreman of the dockers, who is trusted by everyone; he saves the silver, hides it, and is slowly destroyed by the secret of it, while the mine's wealth corrupts the whole society around him and the country passes from one dictator to another.
narrative_structure: Five-part structure moving backward and forward in time, with a large cast whose lives intersect around the mine and the silver.
principal_characters: Nostromo; Charles Gould; Emilia Gould; Martin Decoud; Dr Monygham; Antonia Avellanos; Don José Avellanos
historical_context: The Central American and South American republics of the late nineteenth century, their cycles of revolution and foreign debt, and the imperial economics of the silver mine — Conrad drew on his knowledge of the Latin American revolutions and on the history of the American-financed mines.
literary_significance: Nostromo is the greatest political novel in English of the period: it invented the fictional republic as a model of the whole of politics, its structure of parallel and intersecting lives over decades is one of the most ambitious in the novel, and its analysis of how wealth and foreign capital corrupt every revolutionary ideal has never been surpassed.

title: The Secret Agent: A Simple Tale
description: A Soho shopkeeper in the pay of a foreign embassy plots a bomb attack on Greenwich Observatory, and destroys his own family in the process.
plot_or_argument: Mr Verloc, a lazy Soho shopkeeper who sells pornography and frequents anarchist meetings, is an agent of a foreign embassy. Ordered to stage an outrage against 'the fetish of science', he sends his simple-minded brother-in-law Stevie to carry a bomb to Greenwich; Stevie stumbles and is blown to pieces, and Verloc's wife Winnie, discovering the truth, murders him and is herself destroyed. The novel ends in a fogbound London of police, spies and solitary misery.
narrative_structure: Chronological narrative with a delayed revelation of the murder and a documentary account of London's police and anarchist underworld.
principal_characters: Mr Verloc; Winnie Verloc; Stevie; Adolf Verloc's mother; Chief Inspector Heat; the Assistant Commissioner; Vladimir; Ossipon
historical_context: The anarchist scare and the spy mania of the 1890s, the Greenwich Observatory bombing of 1894 (an actual attempt by a French anarchist), and the London of Soho, the embassy and the detective police.
literary_significance: The Secret Agent is the greatest English novel about terrorism and one of the darkest comedies in the language: it invented the domestic spy novel, has never been equalled in its analysis of the political agent as an ordinary, lazy, frightened man, and the murder of Stevie is one of the most shocking scenes in English fiction.

title: Under Western Eyes
description: The political novel of Russian autocracy and exile: a student informer in St Petersburg and Geneva, and the impossibility of innocence under a police state.
plot_or_argument: Razumov, a St Petersburg student, is approached by a fellow student, Haldin, who has just assassinated a government minister and asks for help; Razumov betrays him to the police and is set to spy on the revolutionary exiles in Geneva. There he falls in love with Haldin's sister Nathalie and is slowly destroyed by guilt, finally confessing to the revolutionaries and being deafened and crippled by their vengeance.
narrative_structure: First-person narrative by an English teacher of languages, with Razumov's diary embedded in it; two unequal parts (Russia, Geneva).
principal_characters: Kirylo Sidorovitch Razumov; Victor Haldin; Nathalie Haldin; Peter Ivanovitch; Sophia Antonovna; Councillor Mikulin
historical_context: The Russian autocracy of the 1900s, the Okhrana, the revolutionary emigration in Geneva and the assassination of the Minister of the Interior Vyacheslav von Plehve (1904); Conrad drew on his Polish family's experience of Russian exile.
literary_significance: Under Western Eyes is the finest English novel about the police state and the moral condition of the informer: it is the direct ancestor of Koestler's Darkness at Noon and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, and its portrait of Razumov is one of the great studies of betrayal and self-knowledge in the language.

title: Tono-Bungay
description: The rise and fall of a patent-medicine fortune and a portrait of England from the 1870s to the 1900s — Wells's finest novel.
plot_or_argument: George Ponderevo, nephew of the fraudulent chemist Edward Ponderevo, recounts his uncle's rise from provincial pharmacist to the owner of the Tono-Bungay patent medicine empire, the family's ascent into the wealthy classes, and its collapse. George's other life as an aeronautical engineer and his flight over Africa give the novel its images of the modern age; the book ends with the uncle ruined and dying and England seen as a system of shams.
narrative_structure: First-person retrospective with a large cast and a documentary survey of English society.
principal_characters: George Ponderevo; Edward Ponderevo; Susan Ponderevo; Marion Ramboat; Beatrice Normandy
historical_context: The patent-medicine boom and the advertising culture of the 1890s, the new wealth of the Edwardian middle class, the failure of English institutions, and the beginnings of aviation.
literary_significance: Tono-Bungay is Wells's masterpiece and one of the great Edwardian condition-of-England novels: it invented the novel of advertising, and its portrait of the sham empire of commerce — the patent medicine as a metaphor for the whole society — is the finest thing Wells wrote.

title: The Outline of History: Being a Plain History of Life and Mankind
description: The whole history of life and mankind in one narrative: the most widely read history book ever written in English, and the foundation of the modern popular history.
plot_or_argument: Wells begins with the formation of the earth, traces the evolution of life, the emergence of the human species, the ancient civilisations, the world religions, the empires, the Renaissance, the Enlightenment, the industrial revolution and the First World War, and closes with an argument for a world state as the only alternative to self-destruction.
narrative_structure: Chronological world survey in forty chapters, from cosmology to the League of Nations.
historical_context: The First World War and the peace settlement, the collapse of the old empires, the League of Nations, and the new mass readership created by cheap printing and the book clubs — the book sold over two million copies in the 1920s.
literary_significance: The Outline of History made history a popular literary form: it sold in millions, created the modern illustrated popular history, and its argument for a single world civilisation made Wells the most influential public intellectual of the period. It is the book that taught the twentieth century its own past.

title: The Shape of Things to Come: The Ultimate Revolution
description: A history of the next two centuries: the collapse of civilisation in a world war, the rise of a technocratic world state, and the flight to the moon.
plot_or_argument: Written as a manuscript by a diplomat of the future, the book narrates a world war beginning in 1940 that destroys civilisation, a plague, a long dark age, the emergence of a technological ruling order, its unification of the world, and the launching of the first lunar expedition — ending with the question of whether humanity will choose the stars or stagnation.
narrative_structure: Future history narrated as a recovered manuscript with a framing preface and footnotes.
principal_characters: Dr Philip Raven; the World Council; the Modern State
literary_form: Future history (based on the film Things to Come, 1936)
historical_context: The rise of fascism, the bomber and the fear of total war, the technocratic and utopian movements of the 1930s, and the new medium of the film (Korda's Things to Come, scripted by Wells, appeared in 1936).
literary_significance: The Shape of Things to Come is Wells's last great utopian statement and the most influential future history of the 1930s: it anticipates the world war, the bombing of cities, the plague and the world state, and its images passed directly into the cinema and into the political imagination of the period.

title: The History of Mr Polly
description: A small draper burns down his own shop, fakes his death and discovers freedom on the road.
plot_or_argument: Alfred Polly, a quarrelsome, incompetent draper in Fishbourne, is trapped in an unhappy marriage and a failing business. He resolves on suicide, but before he can act the shop catches fire; he takes the opportunity to disappear, is presumed dead, and reinvents himself as an inn-keeper and woodsman, fighting a local bully, finding a companion, and finally returning to visit his widow's new marriage.
narrative_structure: Third-person comic narrative with a mock-heroic fight and a deliberate fairy-tale ending.
principal_characters: Alfred Polly; Miriam Polly; the plump woman; Uncle Jim; Johnson
historical_context: The Edwardian drapery trade, the small provincial town and the new mobility of the motor road and the bicycle; Wells's own escape from the draper's shop.
literary_significance: The History of Mr Polly is the funniest and most humane of Wells's social novels: it is the great English novel of the small tradesman's escape, and its comic invention — the burning shop, the fight at the Potwell Inn, Mr Polly's private vocabulary — has made it a permanent English classic.

title: The Old Wives' Tale (Bennett, 1908)
description: The lives of two sisters in the Potteries, from the 1860s to the 1900s: the great English novel of time and provincial endurance.
plot_or_argument: Constance and Sophia Baines grow up in their parents' drapery shop in Bursley. Constance marries the shop's manager and stays in the town; Sophia elopes to Paris with a commercial traveller, is abandoned, and becomes the proprietress of a Paris boarding house. The novel follows them for forty years, through the siege of Paris, the deaths of their parents and husbands, and old age, ending with Constance's death and Sophia's return to the town.
narrative_structure: Four-part chronicle moving chronologically across two generations and two countries.
principal_characters: Constance Baines; Sophia Baines; John Baines; Samuel Povey; Gerald Scales; Chirac; Mr Critchlow
historical_context: The Potteries of the 1860s–1900s, the Franco-Prussian War and the siege of Paris (1870–71), the drapery trade and the chapel culture of the Five Towns.
literary_significance: The Old Wives' Tale is the finest English realist novel of the period and one of the great novels about time: its unglamorous chronicle of two ordinary women over forty years showed what the novel could do with the whole of a life, and it is the book on which Bennett's case against the modernists — that fiction must render the material world exactly — rests.

title: Clayhanger
description: A printer's son in the Potteries struggles against his father and the provincial world, in the finest English novel of the autodidact.
plot_or_argument: Edwin Clayhanger, the shy, intelligent son of a tyrannical printer in Bursley, is taken from school at thirteen to work in the family business. The novel follows his long struggle with his father, his thwarted love for the architect's daughter Hilda Lessways, his education and his slow assumption of the business — a study of provincial ambition that ends with him poised to become the prosperous man his father was.
narrative_structure: Chronological third-person narrative in five parts over some twenty years.
principal_characters: Edwin Clayhanger; Darius Clayhanger; Hilda Lessways; Janet Orgreave; Osmond Orgreave; Big James
historical_context: The Potteries printing trade of the 1870s–90s, the Methodist chapel, the mechanics' institute, and the social ascent of the provincial middle class.
literary_significance: Clayhanger is Bennett's most personal novel and the finest English study of the provincial autodidact: it made the Potteries a literary country and gave the nineteenth-century novel of education a modern, ironic form. With Hilda Lessways and These Twain it forms one of the great English family chronicles.

title: The Man of Property
description: The first Forsyte novel: Soames Forsyte's possession of his wife Irene becomes a study of property as a whole way of life.
plot_or_argument: Soames Forsyte, a solicitor and art collector, builds a house at Robin Hill for his wife Irene, who does not love him. When Irene falls in love with the architect, young Philip Bosinney, Soames sues him for the cost of the house; the lawsuit destroys Bosinney, and Irene leaves Soames. The novel ends with the family's verdict on a marriage conceived as an investment.
narrative_structure: Three-part novel with an interlude; dated sections moving chronologically from 1886 to 1887.
principal_characters: Soames Forsyte; Irene Forsyte; Philip Bosinney; Young Jolyon Forsyte; Old Jolyon Forsyte; June Forsyte
historical_context: The London of the propertied upper middle class in the 1880s, the professional classes and their codes of ownership, and the aesthetic movement's effect on the collecting of pictures.
literary_significance: The Man of Property is the founding novel of the great English family saga and the finest study in English fiction of the mentality of property: its portrait of Soames — the man who owns his wife — gave the language a new term for the possessive temperament and made Galsworthy the period's leading social novelist.

title: Howards End
description: Three families and a house: the definitive Edwardian condition-of-England novel and the source of 'only connect'.
plot_or_argument: The estate of Howards End passes from the Wilcoxes to the Schlegel sisters and back. Margaret Schlegel, the elder sister, marries Henry Wilcox, the philistine businessman, and tries to hold together the world of 'telegrams and anger' and the world of 'books and music'; her sister Helen has an affair with the impoverished clerk Leonard Bast, who dies by a falling bookcase, and the novel ends with the house, a baby, and the possibility of connection.
narrative_structure: Four-part novel with dated chapters; the house as the symbolic centre and the inheritance plot as the mechanism.
principal_characters: Margaret Schlegel; Helen Schlegel; Henry Wilcox; Ruth Wilcox; Leonard Bast; Charles Wilcox; Tibby Schlegel
historical_context: The Edwardian middle class and its property, the motor car's destruction of the countryside, the new class of clerks, the imperial business in Africa (the Wilcoxes' Imperial and West African Rubber Company), and the suffrage movement on its margins.
literary_significance: Howards End is the definitive Edwardian novel and one of the permanent English novels of the century: 'only connect' became the period's moral watchword, its analysis of class and the 'undeveloped heart' has never been bettered, and its portrait of England as a house to be inherited is the finest thing Forster wrote.

title: A Passage to India
description: The great English novel about the empire: an Englishwoman in Chandrapore, the Marabar Caves, and the impossibility of friendship between ruler and ruled.
plot_or_argument: Adela Quested arrives in British India to consider marrying Ronny Heaslop, the city magistrate. She befriends Dr Aziz, who arranges an expedition to the Marabar Caves; in the caves Adela is overcome by a hallucination or an assault and accuses Aziz of attacking her. The trial divides the British and Indian communities, Adela withdraws the charge, and Aziz is acquitted — but the friendships are destroyed, and the novel ends with the two men riding through the Mau jungle and agreeing that they cannot be friends yet, not until the English have been driven out.
narrative_structure: Three titled parts (Mosque, Caves, Temple) over two seasons and two locations.
principal_characters: Dr Aziz; Cyril Fielding; Adela Quested; Mrs Moore; Ronny Heaslop; Professor Godbole; Mrs Turton; Nawab Bahadur
historical_context: British India after the Amritsar Massacre (1919) and under the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms; the Anglo-Indian community and the beginnings of the nationalist movement. Forster's own two journeys in India (1912–13, 1921) supplied the material.
literary_significance: A Passage to India is the greatest English novel about the empire and the last great English novel of the liberal tradition: its three-part structure (Mosque, Caves, Temple), its handling of the unrepresentable in the caves, and its ending — 'not yet' — make it the most complete fictional treatment of the colonial situation in the language.

title: Mrs Dalloway
description: A single June day in London in 1923: Clarissa Dalloway prepares a party while a shell-shocked veteran spirals toward death.
plot_or_argument: Clarissa Dalloway, fifty-two, walks through Westminster buying flowers for the party she is giving that evening. In counterpoint, Septimus Warren Smith, a war veteran with shell shock, walks through the same streets with his Italian wife Lucrezia and is taken to a psychiatrist. The novel moves through the minds of both and of a dozen others by interior monologue and free indirect style, and ends with the party, the news of Septimus's suicide, and Clarissa's recognition of a kinship with him.
narrative_structure: Telescoped single day, alternating between Clarissa's and Septimus's consciousness, with free indirect narration and memory as the main movement.
principal_characters: Clarissa Dalloway; Richard Dalloway; Elizabeth Dalloway; Peter Walsh; Sally Seton; Septimus Warren Smith; Lucrezia Warren Smith; Sir William Bradshaw; Miss Kilman
historical_context: London on a June day in 1923, after the First World War; the suffrage generation's daughters, the Harley Street psychiatrists, the Empire's administrators at luncheon, and the new world of the motor car and the aeroplane writing letters in the sky.
literary_significance: Mrs Dalloway is the central English modernist novel and the finest novel of a single day in the language: it perfected the interior monologue in English, made the ordinary consciousness — the party, the flowers, the memory — the matter of high art, and its treatment of shell shock gave the war's aftermath its most exact literary record.

title: To the Lighthouse
description: Two days ten years apart at a Hebridean holiday house: the Ramsay family, the artist Lily Briscoe, and the war in between.
plot_or_argument: The Ramsay family is on holiday on the Isle of Skye before the war: Mr Ramsay, the philosopher, tyrannises over his family with his need for sympathy; Mrs Ramsay holds them together; Lily Briscoe paints; James longs to go to the lighthouse. The second part, 'Time Passes', records the war and the deaths of Mrs Ramsay, Andrew and Prue in a few pages, and the house's decay. The third returns ten years later, with Lily completing her painting and the surviving Ramsays finally reaching the lighthouse.
narrative_structure: Three parts (The Window, Time Passes, The Lighthouse); a single day, a ten-year interval, and a single morning.
principal_characters: Mr Ramsay; Mrs Ramsay; James Ramsay; Cam Ramsay; Lily Briscoe; Charles Tansley; Augustus Carmichael; Minta Doyle; Paul Rayley
historical_context: The pre-war world of the Cambridge philosopher and the summer house; the First World War as an absence; the changes in women's lives and the death of the Victorian family.
literary_significance: To the Lighthouse is Woolf's most perfectly achieved novel and one of the great English novels of the century: its three-part structure, its rendering of the passage of time and of a mother's presence, and Lily Briscoe's painting — the female artist's struggle to make form — are among the finest things in modern fiction.

title: The Waves
description: Six voices and a seventh, from childhood to death: Woolf's most radical experiment and the most musical of her novels.
plot_or_argument: Six friends — Bernard, Susan, Rhoda, Neville, Jinny and Louis — speak in soliloquies that alternate with interludes describing the sea and a house through a single day. Their voices follow them from childhood through school, love, work and age, and the novel ends with Bernard's long final summary of a life, in which the six voices are absorbed into one and the wave breaks on the shore.
narrative_structure: Nine episodes separated by nine prose interludes describing the sea; each episode is a sequence of soliloquies in the six voices.
principal_characters: Bernard; Susan; Rhoda; Neville; Jinny; Louis; Percival
historical_context: The intellectual world of Cambridge and London in the first decades of the century, and the generation that came of age before and during the First World War.
literary_significance: The Waves is the most radical novel of the period and the summit of Woolf's experimental method: it dispenses with plot, character and narrator in favour of six voices and a lyric structure, and it is the finest English attempt to render consciousness as pure pattern, music and rhythm.

title: Orlando: A Biography
description: A biography across four centuries in which the poet-hero changes sex: the wittiest of the modernist novels and a love letter to Vita Sackville-West.
plot_or_argument: Orlando, a young Elizabethan nobleman, begins as a courtier of Queen Elizabeth I, has an affair with a Russian princess, becomes an ambassador to Constantinople, and falls asleep during a revolution and wakes as a woman. She lives through the eighteenth, nineteenth and twentieth centuries, publishes 'The Oak Tree', marries a sea captain, and arrives in the present with a car and a film contract.
narrative_structure: Six chapters by century, with mock-biographical documentation (prefaces, illustrations, dates).
principal_characters: Orlando; Sasha; Marmaduke Bonthrop Shelmerdine; Nick Greene; Queen Elizabeth; Archduchess Harriet
historical_context: English literary and social history from the Elizabethan age to 1928; the Sackville family and Knole, the great house that could not be inherited by a woman; the lesbian relationship with Vita Sackville-West that the novel celebrates.
literary_significance: Orlando is the wittiest and most playful of the modernist novels and the first great English novel of gender as performance: its hero-heroine's change of sex is a philosophical joke that has become a founding text of queer and feminist criticism, and its panorama of English literary history is one of the funniest things Woolf wrote.

title: Sons and Lovers
description: The first great English novel of working-class childhood: the Morel family, the mining village, and a son torn between his mother and his lovers.
plot_or_argument: Gertrude Morel, a cultivated woman, marries a miner and is disillusioned by his drinking and brutality; she turns her love on her sons. Paul, the second son, is bound to her and unable to love either Miriam, the spiritual girl who loves him, or Clara, the married woman who gives him passion; his mother's death at the end frees him into a desolate, unfinished future.
narrative_structure: Two-part chronological novel of childhood and youth, with the mother's death as the climax.
principal_characters: Paul Morel; Gertrude Morel; Walter Morel; William Morel; Miriam Leivers; Clara Dawes; Baxter Dawes
historical_context: The Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire coalfield of the 1880s and 1890s: the pit village, the miners' strike, the chapel, and the new educational opportunities that took miners' sons into clerkships and art schools.
literary_significance: Sons and Lovers is the first great English novel of working-class experience and the founding text of Lawrence's art: it made the mining village and the miner's family a subject for serious fiction, and its account of a son's possession by his mother gave psychoanalytic criticism its favourite English novel.

title: The Rainbow
description: Three generations of the Brangwen family: the great English novel of marriage, the land and the growth of the self.
plot_or_argument: Tom Brangwen, a Derbyshire farmer, marries Lydia Lensky, a Polish widow; their niece Anna marries Will Brangwen; and their daughter Ursula grows up, falls in love with the soldier Anton Skrebensky, refuses marriage, and at the end looks at a rainbow over the industrial Midlands and sees the possibility of a new life. The novel traces the family's passage from the agricultural world to the modern one.
narrative_structure: Three-part generational chronicle across some sixty years, with a lyric and symbolic structure.
principal_characters: Tom Brangwen; Lydia Lensky; Anna Brangwen; Will Brangwen; Ursula Brangwen; Anton Skrebensky
historical_context: The Nottinghamshire–Derbyshire border and the industrialisation of the Midlands from the 1840s to the 1900s; the new education of women, the Boer War, and the crisis of belief.
literary_significance: The Rainbow is Lawrence's greatest novel and one of the finest English novels of the century: it made the family chronicle a vehicle for a philosophy of the self, its prose is the most rhythmically alive in English fiction, and its portrait of a woman's growth into independence is one of the great achievements of the period. Its suppression as obscene in 1915 is one of the century's most notorious acts of censorship.
bibliographical_notes: Suppressed on publication in 1915 after a prosecution for obscenity; the unexpurgated text was not published in Britain until 1968.
